new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (Ko has no catalog record and no statement held by the project). What the work adds is only a group-level, second-hand typological remark (stress-prominent rather than purely pitch-based, per Stevenson) with no placement rule and no Ko data; it is not a catalog-ready placement statement. It sits uneasily with Quint 2020 (held by the project, read: 'probably all Kordofanian languages are tone languages', silent on stress) but does not contradict any placement claim because none exists.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level and second-hand (quoting R. C. Stevenson 1956-57): in the Koalib-Moro / Talodi-Masakin / Lafofa class languages (the group to which Ko = Fungor/Kau/Nyaro belongs in Tucker & Bryan's classification) dynamic stress, co-occurring with high or low tone, is said to matter more than syllabic pitch, with its prominence varying from language to language; the role of tone is 'not yet fully investigated' and a few lexical tone doublets are cited (Laro, Masakin). No statement of WHERE stress falls, no weight or morphological conditioning, and the chapter's examples are unmarked for tone and stress. Ko/Fungor/Kau/Nyaro is not named anywhere in the 1966 volume according to the compilers' full-text searches (the name occurs only in the 1956 Handbook), so nothing here is Ko-specific.
new_statements.exceptions: only that stress 'is not equally prominent in all languages' of the group; no language-by-language detail recoverable from the snippets
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's statement is for their 'class languages' unit 18a (Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin, Lafofa) as a whole, second-hand from Stevenson's Nuba Mountains survey, whose own fieldwork centred on Otoro (with MacDiarmid material); Ko (Fungor, with Kau and Nyaro; Werni sometimes attached) is a member of their Koalib-Moro group per the 1956 Handbook but is not itself named or exemplified in the 1966 chapter, so nothing recovered is specific to any Ko variety.

tone_statements.quote: The principal source for all Heiban data in the lists is [Schadeberg 1981]. Since his transcription is largely based on the IPA, we have preserved it almost intact, with cosmetic differences concerning IPA > UTS transliteration (ʃ > š, c > ɕ, etc.). Doubled vowels in Schadeberg's transcription, marking length, have been converted to single vowels plus the length sign (aa > aː, etc.). Tonal systems in the languages usually involve two registers, and the low register in Schadeberg's transcriptions usually remains unmarked; we consistently mark it with the low tone diacritic (V̀).

sources.note: Secondhand (all Ko data from Schadeberg 1981: 22-56). States that tonal systems in the Heiban languages usually involve two registers and that Schadeberg leaves the low register unmarked, which the GLD re-marks with a grave accent; the 105 Ko forms are accordingly transcribed with high (acute) and low (grave) tone marks (39 acute, 18 grave diacritics counted on the Ko note lines). No Ko-specific statement on tone rules, contours, downstep or stress.
